parole.significato: Placename suffix found in northern Germany
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bēke, from Old Saxon beki, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Doublet of -bach.

parole.significato: place name suffix found in northern Germany
parole.testo: From Middle Low German, from Old Saxon, from the dative plural of a derivative (*būriją?) of Proto-Germanic *būraz (“dwelling”). Cognate with Dutch -buren and perhaps English byre (“barn”). Also related with dated German Bauer (“cage”).

parole.significato: forms adverbs that describe the manner of an action, particularly a movement
parole.testo: From Middle High German -lingen, from Old High German lingūn. The modern form with -s is of Central and Low German origin; compare Middle Low German -linges.

parole.significato: A placename suffix found chiefly in the northern Rhineland.
parole.testo: From Old High German rot (“clearing”), related to roden. The spelling with -a- reflects dialectal [ɔː] in these names. However, most Rhenish dialects should regularly have short [ɔ] (Central Franconian rodde), so there probably underlies some kind of analogy or older form of pronunciation. Another p

parole.significato: Used to form the plurals of some nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Reinforced by the fact that French and English also use -s as a plural suffix.

parole.significato: Placename suffix found in northern Germany.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German -(e)sen, contraction of -hûsen. Thus a byform of German -hausen, which occurs in the same areas in seemingly random variation. Compare -trop, -trup, another Low German contraction that has often survived unaltered.
From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch -te, from Proto-Germanic *-iþō, whence also inherited but equally rare German -de.

parole.significato: Placename suffix found chiefly in north-western Germany
parole.testo: With metathesis in the weakened ultima from Middle Low German dorp (“village”), from Old Saxon thorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą. While Low German placenames in -dorp were generally standardized with the High German equivalent -dorf, those with the less transparent variant -trop, -trup often remaine

parole.significato: to pay compensation to; (by extension) to satisfy
parole.testo: From the Middle Low German verb and construct affinden. Equivalent to ab- + finden.

parole.significato: callous and cunning; experienced in “the game”, in immoral behaviour
parole.testo: Attested from the 16th century. Formally, ab (“off”) + gebrüht (“scalded, boiled”), based on the idea that things are hardened or “steeled” by boiling (e.g. eggs, compare hartgesotten, English hard-boiled). At the same time, perhaps originally, from vulgar Middle Low German brǖden (“to fuck”, also i
Originally "remote place", at first in Middle Low German afort (16th century). The contemporary sense as a euphemism since the 18th century. Analysable as ab (“off, away”) + Ort (“place”).

parole.significato: someone who repairs old shoes (cobbler), clothes (tailor) etc. (male or unspecified sex)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German ōltvlicker. By surface analysis, alt + Flicker.
Borrowed from Middle Low German anrüchtig. See Gerücht for more.
Spread by Luther, possibly a calque of Middle Low German up dat. Compare Dutch opdat (which unlike the German is in general popular use).

parole.significato: to clear up, to turn clear (sky)
parole.testo: Calque of Middle Low German upklāren.

parole.significato: to clear up, explain (a mystery etc)
parole.testo: From auf- + klären, a calque of Middle Low German upklāren. Compare also Dutch opklaren.
From Middle High German ūfruor, from Middle Low German uprōr. Compare Dutch oproer, English uproar.
From ausbündig, from Middle Low German ūtbundich.
Calque of Middle Low German ūtbundich.

parole.significato: outside the dyke, in front of it, located towards the water
parole.testo: From außen + Deich + -s, a calque of Middle Low German bûtendîkes. Compare Dutch buitendijks.
Borrowed from Middle Low German ūtstafferen, equivalent to aus- + staffieren.

Attested a few times in Old High German, but only much later effectively introduced via Middle Low German ūster, from Middle Dutch oester. The Dutch word is borrowed from Latin ostrea, itself from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon) (pertaining to ὀστέον (ostéon, “bone”), ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “shell”)).

parole.significato: forecastle (raised part of the upper deck)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German bak (“bowl, box, chest”), from Middle Dutch bak (modern Dutch bak), from Old French bac (“large bowl”). Related with Becken, but unrelated with Backbord. The sense “dining table” is due to the fact that several sailors would eat from one bowl, so the word Back came to be used

parole.significato: port (the left side of a ship when facing the fore)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German backbort, bakbort (15th c.). Compare Dutch bakboord (1599), Old English bæcbord (ca. 885).
17th century, from backen (“bake”) + Stein (“stone”), a calque of Middle Low German backstên.
17th century, from Middle Low German bāke, from Old Frisian bāken, from Proto-West Germanic *baukn, from Proto-Germanic *baukną. Cognate with Dutch baak, English beacon.
Borrowed from Middle Low German ballast, a compound word the second part of which is Last. The origin of the first part is uncertain; several theories and possible paths of borrowing are discussed.

parole.significato: to bang (make a loud, dull sound)
parole.testo: From Late Middle High German bollern, from Middle Low German balderen, (with Low German -ld- → -ll-). Compare Dutch bolderen and bulderen. However, independent onomatopoeia is equally possible. The football sense via “to shoot” and through secondary association with Ball (“ball”). See also Bollerwag

parole.significato: The beak of a bird of prey.
parole.testo: From Middle Low German beck, probably through Dutch bek, from Middle Dutch bec, from Middle French bec (“beak”) or Old French bec, from Vulgar Latin beccus, probably from Gaulish. Compare modern French bec, English beak.

parole.significato: A kind of mediaeval and early-modern tax in some German regions.
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German bede and Middle Low German bēde, from Proto-Germanic *bedō (“plea”). Doublet of Bitte (“plea”). The use for a tax developed in Middle High German.

parole.significato: preaching bands (a kind of neckwear worn chiefly by Protestant ministers)
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German beve, beffe, itself (possibly via Middle Dutch) from Old French biffe (“striped fabric”). Compare Dutch bef.

parole.significato: perplexed; in a sudden state of confusion (e.g. through a lack of concentration, or shock)
parole.testo: Past participle of the rarer verb belämmern or belemmern (“to annoy", "to molest”), from Middle Low German belemmeren. The verb pertains to lahm (“lame”) and is cognate with Dutch belemmeren (“to hamper”). The semantic development of the adjective in German is, at least in part, due to association w

From Middle High German bequæme, bekōme (“suitable”), from Old High German biquāmi, derived from biqueman (whence German bekommen). The word seems originally to have been more common in Central and Low German; therefore possibly reinforced by cognate Middle Low German bequēme. The consonantism -qu-,

Borrowed from Middle Low German bernstein, barnstēn. Pertaining to brennen (“to burn”) with Low German metathesis of -r- (compare bersten, Born). Cognate with English brimstone and Old Norse brennisteinn. The word was borrowed from Middle Low German into several Scandinavian and Slavic languages.
Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?], related to rufen. See Gerücht for more.

Borrowed from Middle Low German beschênigen (14th c.), extended form of beschênen, from be- + Proto-West Germanic *skainijan (“to make appear”). This latter verb is a causative of *skīnan, whence German scheinen (“to shine, appear”). It was borrowed along the Lower Rhine in the 15th century and full

From Middle High German besudeln, besodeln, besodelen, equivalent to be- + Sudel (“puddle; muck”), from Middle Low German sudde (“swamp; marsh”). Akin to Middle High German sutte (“puddle; mudhole”), Old English ġesyd (“wallowing hole”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German bête, from Old Saxon *bēta, from Proto-West Germanic *bētā (“beet”).

parole.significato: to run, to operate (a business, an engine, etc.)
parole.testo: From be- + treiben. A calque of Middle Low German bedrīven.

parole.significato: operating or running a technical device, application or process, in other words planful activity under the exploitation…
parole.testo: A calque of Middle Low German bedrîf, like the underlying verb betreiben (from bedrîven). The noun is closer to the Low German form because of the preserved monophthong (instead of *Betreib). See the regular development in cognate Dutch bedrijf.

From late Middle High German biute, borrowed from Middle Low German büte, whence also the forms in other languages like Dutch buit, English booty, French butin. Of uncertain ultimate origin; possibly a Celtic borrowing, from Proto-Celtic *boudi (“victory, booty, spoils”). If so, related to the name
From Middle High German biuten (“to treat something as booty”), borrowed from Middle Low German bûten (“to plunder”). By surface analysis, Beute (“booty”) + -n.

Enhanced form of earlier bezichten (15th c.), denominal from now obsolete Bezicht (“accusation”), from Middle High German beziht, itself deverbal from Old High German bezīhan. Modern German bezeihen was gradually displaced, but is still attested until the early 20th century. The form with -ig- (16th
From Middle Low German bikbēre, bickbēre. By surface analysis, German Low German Pick (“pitch”) + Beere (“berry”).

parole.significato: animal, beast, any kind but especially an annoying one, e.g. an insect, pest, aggressive dog, etc.
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German and/or West Central German from Middle Dutch beest, itself from Old French beste, from Latin bēstia. Doublet of Bestie.

parole.significato: to jingle; to chime (make the sound of a small bell)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German bimmeln, of onomatopoeic origin.

From Middle Low German binnen (“within”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“by, at”) + *innan << *in (“in”). The form is also Central German in Middle High German binnen (compare Luxembourgish bannen). It is originally an adverb meaning “within, inside” chiefly in local sense, equivalent to Germ
From Middle Low German binnen (“within”). See binnen for more.

parole.significato: inside the dyke, behind it, located towards the hinterland
parole.testo: From binnen + Deich + -s, a calque of Middle Low German binnendîkes. Compare Dutch binnendijks.

From Middle High German bloc, from Old High German bloc. The more common Middle High German form was originally bloch, from Old High German bloh. The variant prevailed in modern German under the reinforcing influence of Middle Low German block. All from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germani

15th century, from Middle High German bole, or from or akin to Middle Low German bōle (“thick board”, 14th c.), probably from Proto-Germanic *bulaz (“trunk; plank”), and ultimately related to Ball (“ball”). Cognate with Middle Dutch bolle, Old Norse bolr (see there for more), English bole (all “tree
Borrowed from Middle Low German bōnen, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”). Cognate with Dutch boenen.
Via Middle Low German from early modern Dutch boye. Compare contemporary Dutch boei, English buoy.

parole.significato: upper leg, thigh (including the buttock), especially when sturdy or fleshy, now most often said of slaughtered poultry
parole.testo: Of dialectal origin, from Middle Low German bolle m or f, which is the same word as Bolle f (“roundish object”, etymology 2). The sense “thigh” probably developed under influence of (remotely related) Middle Low German bille, for which see Dutch bil (“buttock”).
From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bolwerk.
Via Middle Low German bōt, from Middle English bot (compare modern English boat).
15th century, borrowed from Middle Low German bort, from Old Saxon bord, from Proto-West Germanic *bord. Ultimately the same word as in etymology 2 above.
Borrowed from Middle Low German borke, from Proto-Germanic *barkuz. Cognate with Dutch and English bark.
Low and Central German form of Brunnen with r-metathesis. From northern Middle High German born and Middle Low German born(e). See the same in Bernstein, bersten.
Borrowed from Middle Low German bras (“din, racket”), related to prassen.

A Central and Low German form with -ss- for -chs-, from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German brassem, from Old High German brahsma, from Proto-West Germanic *brahsima, from Proto-Germanic *brahsmǭ, perhaps from *brehwanaz (“shining, glittery, sparkly”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerek-

Borrowed from Middle Low German brēgen, from Old Saxon *bregin, *bragan, from Proto-West Germanic *bragn, from Proto-Germanic *bragną. Cognate with Old English bræġn / bræġen, Dutch brein, English brain.
From Middle High German bremse, borrowed from Middle Low German premese (“twitch for horses”), from the verb pramen (“to clamp”), with further origin unclear (DWDS).

parole.significato: horsefly, breezefly, gadfly (fly of the family Tabanidae)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German brēmse, borrowed from Old Saxon *brimissa, from *brummōn, from Proto-West Germanic *brummōn (“to buzz, drone”). This form superseded High German Breme (now archaic), from Middle High German breme, from Old High German brema. The form brimissa did exist in Old High German, but
Buche + Weizen. A calque of Middle Low German bōkwete.

parole.significato: groyne, breakwater (dam extending perpendicularly into the water to protect the shore)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German būne (“groyne, breakwater”). Possibly related to Bühne.
Via German Low German from Middle Low German bulle. Cognate with Dutch bul. More at bull.

parole.significato: a hill of dry terrain in bog or marshland
parole.testo: 16th century, from Middle Low German bult, bülte, from Proto-West Germanic *bulti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blow, inflate, swell”). Cognate with Dutch bult.
Via Middle Low German buxe (seemingly from *bock-hose; see Hose). Also a West Central German word; compare Ripuarian Botz, Luxembourgish Box.

parole.significato: to bawl; to bellow; to roar
parole.testo: From Middle Low German belken, probably ultimately imitative. Compare blöken. Compare further Dutch balken, English belch.

From Middle Low German bönhase, bonehase (“cat”), from böne (“loft, attic”) + hase (“hare”), the former being cognate of German Bühne (“stage”). The word is first attested in the early 14th century as a personal name (and is thus probably even older). Since the 15th century it meant “illegally worki

parole.significato: fertile plain (usually one within the North European Plain)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German borde. Cognate with English border, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board”). A Börde is usually linear and borders on higher ground.

In its modern form pertaining to Bottich (“tub”), but not directly related to it. Instead from Middle Low German bödeker with the Low German suffix -ker from böde (“barrel”) (compare Bütt); in early modern German (East Central German) adapted to the High German consonantism as botticher (at that tim
From Middle High German bückinc, borrowed from Middle Low German bückink. Pertaining to Bock (“buck”), seemingly because of the pungent smell.

From Middle High German bürgerschaft, equivalent to Bürger (“citizen”) + -schaft (“-ship, -ry”). The sense “municipal parliament” after Middle Low German börgerschop (“municipal council”). Compare also Dutch burgerschap.

From Dach (“roof”) + Hase (“hare”). Attested in this form at least since the 17th century. The word is either an alteration of Middle Low German bönhase (“cat”, literally “loft hare”), which is found in the early 14th century (as a name and thus probably even older), or both words must go back to so

parole.significato: to last, to continue, to persist (for a period of time)
parole.testo: From Middle High German dūren, borrowed from Middle Low German dūren, itself from Latin dūrō. Compare Dutch duren, English dure.
From Middle Low German dûne, from Old Norse dúnn. The diphthong -au- is a secondary adaptation from the Low German to the standard German vowel system.

From Middle Low German dīk, from Old Saxon dīk, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz. Originally the same word as Teich (“pond”). The sense “dike” spread via Low German, for which reason the form Deich is most often regarded as an artificial adaptation of Middle Low German dīk (

parole.significato: punishment, reprehension, beating (most often: so as to intimidate and deter)
parole.testo: denken + Zettel, literally “think note”. At first in Middle Low German denkcēdel (“judicial certificate”).

Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dingesdach, dinsdach and Middle Dutch dinsendach (both with variants), and gradually replaced Middle High German ziestac and other High German forms like Alemannic German Zischtig or Bavarian Ertag. Only since the second half of the 17th. century
Borrowed from Middle Low German dolle, from Proto-Germanic *þullaz (“thole, rowlock”).

parole.significato: cod (marine fish of the family Gadidae)
parole.testo: From Middle High German dorsch, borrowed from Middle Low German dorsch, itself from Old Norse þorskr, from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz.

parole.significato: box (container made from metal or plastic, less often wood)
parole.testo: Spread via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German dōse and Middle Dutch dose. Probably from Latin dosis (“dose”), with semantic shift "a small amount (dose) of medicine" > "a container of such a dose of medicine" > "containers in general".

parole.significato: bold, brash, audacious, impudent (without respect or restraint)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German drîste, from Old Saxon thrīsti, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīstī.
Derived from Middle Low German drīstichēt. Analyzable as dreist + -igkeit.

Seemingly from Middle Low German and/or Middle Dutch drillen, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *þurhil (“perforated, hole”). The verb may have existed in Middle High German, but only a strong past participle gedrollen (“round”) is attested. The Upper German dialects have a verb trillen, whi

Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German drōne (variant of commoner drāne), from Old Saxon drāna, from Proto-West Germanic *drānu, from Proto-Germanic *drēnuz. The Low German form replaced older Tren(e), Trän(e), from Middle High German trën(e), from Old High German trëno, from the Germanic ablaut variant *

parole.significato: reeve, sheriff, bailiff (official in charge of a rural district)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German droste, from earlier drossete, drotsēte, drotsāte. Cognate with Dutch drost and Middle High German truhtsæze, whence the doublet Truchsess (“steward of a princely household, sewer”). See there for more.

Borrowed from Middle Low German drȫge (“dry”), from Old Saxon *drōgi, from Proto-Germanic *draugiz. Also a Central German form; compare Ripuarian drüch, Luxembourgish dréchen (“dry”). Related to Upper German trocken and, in early modern German, used as a mere dialectal variant of it. In the contempo
From Middle High German tucken, tücken. Pertains to tauchen (“to dive”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German ducken). Related to English duck.

parole.significato: audacious, reckless (impudent, stupid, inappropriate through lacking consideration); generally of speech or social beha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from the Middle Low German compound dumdrīste, in which dum (dumm) did not mean "stupid" but rather "reckless". Later interpreted more literally as dumm + dreist, literally “dumb-brash”.
Borrowed from Middle Low German. Related to dösen (“to doze”).

Via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch dûne, from Old Dutch dūna, from Proto-Germanic *dūnǭ. Middle Dutch origin is assured by the German -ü- (compare Süden). The more common Middle Low German form was dûne (with a back vowel -u-); this form may be originally Low German or an earlier borrowing from

From Middle Low German dûster, from Old Saxon thiustri, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *þiustrī (“dark, without light”). The word also exists in parts of West Central German (compare Luxembourgish däischter), which probably facilitated the borrowing; but the standardised form is definitely from
16th century, from Middle Low German ebbe, from Old Saxon *ebbia, from Proto-West Germanic *abbjā, from Proto-Germanic *abjǭ. Cognate to Dutch eb, English ebb.
Borrowed from Middle Low German ebben; see Ebbe.

From Middle High German echt, borrowed from Middle Low German echt (“lawful, genuine”). The original form is Middle Low German ēhaft (“lawful”), from ē (“law”) (related to modern Ehe); then ēhacht by the Low German development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte); and eventually contracted into echt. Cogna

parole.significato: an island, usually a small and/or isolated one
parole.testo: From Middle High German eilant, einlant, from Middle Low German eilant (by which it was reinforced again during the 16th c.), from Old Frisian eiland, from Proto-West Germanic *auwjuland, from Proto-Germanic *awjōlandą. Cognate with Dutch eiland, English island, Icelandic eyland.
From Middle High German eintraht, which is a borrowing and phonetic adaptation of Middle Low German ēndracht. By surface analysis, ein (“one”) + Tracht (“load, burden”).
From Middle Low German ēkel, probably from the verb in German ekeln, which see.

15th century, from Middle Low German ēgelen, ēchelen, ēkelen, from Old Saxon *eglan, from Proto-West Germanic *aglijan (related to English ail). The -k- then likely through influence of Middle Low German ēken, āken (“to suppurate”), from Old Saxon *akan (related to English ache); compare Dutch akeli
17th century, from entbehren (“to lack, be deprived”) + -ung, probably after Middle Low German entbēringe (15th c.). Compare Dutch ontbering (16th c.).
Borrowed from Middle Low German entlanc, cognate with German in lang (with a gliding sound -t-).

Partly from Middle High German esch, ezzisch, from Old High German ezzisc, and partly from Middle Low German esch, *etsch, from Old Saxon etisk, all from Proto-Germanic *atiska- (“grainfield”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂edos- (“sort of cereal, grain”), related to Latin ador (“spelt”), Hit

From Ulenspiegel (1st half of the 16th century), Middle Low German Ūlenspēgel. Its modern semantics is due to the mischievous nature of Till Eulenspiegel, protagonist of a folklore published in 1515. By surface analysis, Eule + -n- + Spiegel, literally “owl mirror”, an analysis already drawn upon in
Compound of fahren (“travel”) + Zeug (“equipment”), which is a calque of Middle Low German vārtüch. The word was originally restricted to vessels, as still is Dutch vaartuig.

From Middle Low German venne, from Old Saxon fenni, from Proto-West Germanic *fani, from Proto-Germanic *fanją. The word did exist in High German (Old High German fenni), but Middle High German venne is rare and the word was later lost in Upper German and most dialects of Central German. The modern
Borrowed from Middle Low German vette; see fett for more.
From Middle Low German vet, from Old Saxon *fētid, from Proto-West Germanic *faitid. Doublet of feist. In the colloquial sense perhaps a calque of English phat via hip-hop culture.

parole.significato: big dorsal fin as found in large fish and marine mammals
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German finne, vinne, from Old Saxon *finna, from Proto-Germanic *finnō. More at fin.

parole.significato: a hanging lower lip or grimacing corner of the mouth
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German flabbe. Cognate to English flap, Dutch flap.

Via Middle Low German flau, from Middle Dutch vlau (compare modern Dutch flauw). The Dutch word was borrowed from Old French flou (“tired, weary”), which is probably of Germanic origin and, if so, then cognate with German lau.
From Middle Low German vlûsch (“sheepskin”), ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *fleus (“fleece”). Doublet of Flause and Fluse.

Borrowed from Middle Low German vlūs, vlūsch (“sheepskin”) or a derivative thereof, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *fleus (“fleece”). The figurative sense may have been derived from “flock of wool” via “worthless thing”. The same word was later borrowed again in its original sense as Flus
Borrowed from Middle Low German flebbe. Cognate to English flap, Dutch flap.

Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German vlêder, vlider (“elder”), itself probably from Middle Dutch vlieder, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *fleuþr. Cognate with modern Dutch vlier, West Frisian flear. At first merely a northern synonym of Holunder (“elder”); then in the 18th century transferred to th

Borrowed from Middle Low German vlīse, from Proto-Germanic *flīsō (“split chip”), a nasalized dental extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)pley- (“to split, splice”), whence also Proto-Germanic *splītaną (“to split”). Cognate with Swedish flis (“wood chips”) (DWDS).
From Middle Low German vlint.
Borrowed from Middle Low German flitse, flitsche, Dutch flitse, both borrowed from Middle French fleche (“arrow”), from Vulgar Latin *fleccia.
Via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch vlot (“afloat, floatable”). Ultimately from the root of fließen (“to flow”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German vlōte, which pertains to fließen (“to flow”). The contemporary form is modelled on French flotte.

parole.significato: line, alignment (vertical or horizontal line along which houses, walls, windows or other building elements are arranged)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German vlucht, from Old Saxon fluht, from Proto-West Germanic *fluhti (“flying”). Pertaining to fliegen (“to fly”).

15th century (East Prussian), also vluder, from Middle Low German vlundere, from Old Saxon *flunthria, eventually from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. The High German word must be from Low German given the marine context. However, Low German attestations are equally late and there are some indications th

Borrowed from Middle Low German vlügge in the 15th or 16th century, eventually completely displacing its High German equivalent flück, possibly motivated by better matching the consonantism of related fliegen.

Borrowed from Middle Low German vorke, from Old Saxon furka, from Proto-West Germanic *furkō, from Latin furca. The word did originally exist in High German (already Old High German furka), but the modern use is based on the Low German lineage and chiefly restricted to originally Low German areas. C
From Middle Low German vracht, alongside vrecht. The form with -a- (see also Dutch vracht) may ultimately be from Old Frisian.
17th century, from Middle Low German vrachten (compare Middle Dutch vrachten). By surface analysis, Fracht + -en.
Fracht (“freight”) + Schiff (“ship”), after Middle Low German vrachtschip.

Originally restricted to Low and Central German; generalized by Luther. Borrowed from Middle Low German vrien and Middle High German vrīen, frīen, vrijen, vrigen, from Old High German *frīon; compare Old Saxon friohon. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *frijōną. Cognate to Dutch vrijen.
From Middle High German vuhsswanz, from Middle Low German vosswanz. By surface analysis, Fuchs (“fox”) + Schwanz (“tail”).

parole.significato: to fumble (idly touch or nervously handle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German fummelen, fimmelen, perhaps ultimately imitative of fumbling. Or, from Proto-Indo-European *pal- (“to shake, swing”), see also Latin palpō (“to pat, touch softly”), and possibly Proto-Germanic *fōlijaną (“to feel”). Cognate with English fumble.

parole.significato: eyelet; hole for a rope or hook
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą. Cognate with Dutch gat, English gate. Doublet of Gate.
Borrowed from Middle Low German geck (“fool”). The same word has later been borrowed again from Ripuarian as jeck (“crazy”) and Jeck (“fool; carnival reveler”).

From Middle High German geverte (“way, ride, walk, behaviour”), from Old High German *giferti (attested as giverte, etc.), from faran, whence modern fahren. The contemporary sense (17th c.) after cognate Middle Low German gevērde.

From Middle Low German gēgenēre, which is derived from a verb gēgenen (“to face, encounter”). Compare German begegnen. Ultimately pertaining to gegen (“against”). Cognate to Dutch jegener (“opponent”). Compare English gainer.

Borrowed (and phonetically adapted) from Middle Low German gelach, gelōch. Pertaining to legen (“to lay”) and hence originally “food and drink laid on the table”. Now often associated more closely with liegen (“to lie”) and interpreted as “party where people lie down drunk”. Compare Dutch gelag.

Inherited from Middle High German gerüchte (Central German), borrowed from Middle Low German geruchte, gerüchte. This northern form replaced earlier Middle High German geruofte, gerüefte, from Old High German geruofti. The noun ultimately pertains to the verb rufen (“to call”) (Old High German ruofa

parole.significato: tides (periodic change of the sea level)
parole.testo: From the plural of Middle High German gezīt (“particular time, such as a feast or prayer time”), from Old High German gizit (“passage of time”), from gi- + zit. The modern sense is loaned from cognate Middle Low German getīde, whence also Tide. Related to Zeit.

parole.significato: to desire greedily, to lust for
parole.testo: From Middle High German or Middle Low German gīren (“to open one’s jaws, gape, scream”), from Proto-Germanic *gīran- and ultimately imitative. Cognate with Dutch gieren (“to scream”). Related also with German Geier (“vulture”) and gähnen, English yawn. In standard German, the word has always been as

From Middle High German and Old High German gires. A chiefly Central German word, later reinforced by cognate Middle Low German gerse. Further origin unknown. Likely related with Lithuanian garšva (“ground elder”).
17th century, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch gilde. Related to Geld and gelten, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *geldan (“to pay”).
From Middle Low German glibberich, from a Proto-Germanic base derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“to shine”). Compare Dutch glibberig, English glibbery.

parole.significato: to look with big eyes; to eye
parole.testo: Expanded form of Middle Low German glupen.
Borrowed from Middle Low German gnitte, from Old Saxon *gnitta, from Proto-Germanic *gnittaz, *gnattaz (“gnat, midge”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰneHdʰn-, *gʰneHd- (“to gnaw, scratch”).

From Gras (“grass”) + Hüpfer (“hopper”). A chiefly northern word, partly from Middle Low German grashüppel (and variants). Not attested in continental West Germanic before the 16th century, but considering Old English græshoppa perhaps older. Compare the similar motivation in German Heuschrecke.

parole.significato: to grumble (make a low sound, as of a discontent person, an empty stomach, a distant thunderstorm)
parole.testo: From Low and Central German dialects, from Middle Low German grummelen and northern Middle High German *grummeln, iterative of grummen. A relation with Gram and grimmig is theoretically possible, but the words certainly have a strong onomatopoeic element. Cognate with Dutch grommelen, English grumbl

parole.significato: gruit (herbal mixture used in some beers, particularly before the spread of hops)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German grūt, from Old Saxon grūt, from Proto-Germanic *grūtą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to rub, grind”). Cognate with Dutch gruit (whence English gruit), English grout.

From Middle High German grēslich, from Middle Low German grēselîk (“horrific”), probably ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *grīsan (“to be frightened”), which is cognate with Old English grislic, whence English grisly. Cognate with Bavarian greißlich. In High German associated with unrelated graz

parole.significato: Any fish of the genus Gobio, especially a common gudgeon (Gobio gobio)
parole.testo: Central and Low German alteration of the word in Grundel (now defined as “goby”), at first in Middle Low German grundelingk (early 15th c.).

15th century, from Middle Low German hakke, from Proto-Germanic *hak(k)-, perhaps related to *hakô. Cognate with Dutch hak. The word also existed in Old High German as hakka (“animal heel”), but this had no attested continuation in Middle High German.

From Middle Low German havene. The word was already borrowed into Middle High German habene; the modern form with -f- is a later adaptation once again based on the Middle Low German form. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *habnō. Cognate to Dutch haven and English haven.

From Middle High German hafer, haber, hafere, habere, from Old High German habaro. The modern consonantism is Central German (compare Middle Low German haver, havere and modern German Low German Haver, Hafer). The Upper German cognate form Haber is now obsolete in standard usage.

Borrowed from Middle Low German hanenrey. The word is also attested in Middle High German [Term?], but it was rare and the later spread was without doubt based on Low German. The original sense seems to have been “capon”, that is a castrated cock. Further etymology unsettled. Compare Swedish hanrej,
From Middle High German and Middle Low German hame, from Old High German hamo (“tunnel net, wrap”).

From Middle High German hantieren, which is borrowed—probably via Middle Low German—from Middle Dutch hanteren, itself from Old French hanter (“to frequent someone”). The Old French word is usually traced back Old Norse heimta (“to bring home”). The semantic development in German is based on popular
Borrowed from Middle Low German harke. Cognate with Dutch hark. Compare also French herque (“metal rake”).

From Middle High German harren, further origin is unclear. Popularised by Luther. Perhaps borrowed from Middle Low German harren, harden (“to wait, await”), from Old Saxon *hardōn (“to become hard, harden, be steadfast, await”), from Proto-West Germanic *hardēn (“to become hard, endure, wait, persev

16th century, from Middle Low German hāst, from Middle Dutch haest, a borrowing from Old French haste, itself borrowed from Frankish *hai(f)st, from Proto-Germanic *haifstiz. See English haste for more.

parole.significato: accident, emergency (most often of a ship); shipwreck
parole.testo: Via Middle Low German haverye from early modern Dutch haverij (modern averij), from French avarie, Italian avaria, from Arabic عَوَارِيَّة (ʕawāriyya). Compare contemporary Dutch averij. Doublet of average.

parole.significato: to pant or breathe fast and loudly through one’s mouth (much like dogs do when hot or short of breath)
parole.testo: An onomatopoeic word liable to alteration and variation. Formally iterative of obsolete hechen, heichen (“to pant”), a chiefly Central and Low German word; compare Middle Low German hīgen, heigen, hēgen (“to pant”), from or related with Proto-West Germanic *hīgōn (whence Dutch hijgen, English hie).

From Middle Low German heck (“wooden fencing”), from Old Saxon *hekki, from Proto-West Germanic *hakkju. The sense “back of a ship” because the position of the helmsman in the stern was enclosed by such a fence. Cognate to Dutch hek, English hatch.

parole.significato: hards, tow, oakum (short, fallen-off fibres of flax or hemp)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hêde, from Proto-West Germanic *heʀdā. Cognate with English hards, which see.

Probably a dialectal variant of Middle Low German ēkel (“disgusting”), from which German Ekel (“loathing, disgust, fastidiousness”). A connection to Proto-Germanic *aikulaz (“fearful”) has been suggested for both words; compare Old English acol (“burdensome, troublesome”), English ache, Galician ext

From Middle High German helle(n)barte, from older helmbarte, from helm (“stalk”) + barte (“axe”). The modern -d- is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German hēlenbārde) and/or influenced by French hallebarde, itself from the Middle High German. parole.significato: to feign (friendship, morality, etc.); to be hypocritical
parole.testo: Spread by Luther; origin unsettled. Probably from Middle Low German hüchelen (whence Danish hykle and Swedish hyckla), which may be akin to Old English hīewian. From Middle Low German hūre, from Old Saxon huria (“hire”). Cognate to Dutch huur.
From Middle Low German *hürling, from Old Saxon *hūriling, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijuling. Compare English hireling, Dutch huurling.
Borrowed from Middle Low German hüren, from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijan.

16th century, from Middle Low German hissen, of unknown origin. Possibly the same word as Middle Low German hissen, hitzen, Middle Dutch hissen (modern Dutch ophitsen), Old French hicier, all meaning “to set hounds on”. These can be compared to Proto-Germanic *hatjaną (whence High German hetzen), bu

parole.significato: rail, bar (on which to hold on to)
parole.testo: Probably from Middle Low German holm (“girt”), from Old Saxon *helma, from Proto-West Germanic *helmō, which pertains to the Germanic root *helmô (compare English helm). Older theories derive it from the plural of dialectal Hulbe (“beam”) with -ben → -m (a rather common development in German). This

Borrowed from Middle Low German and Old Saxon holm (“island”), from Proto-West Germanic *holm. Cognate with English holm, Danish holm, Swedish holme, Icelandic hólmi. Doublet of Kulm (“rounded mountaintop”).

parole.significato: a small cluster of farms, often no more than three to five
parole.testo: From Middle Low German hôk (“corner, angle”), from Old Saxon hōk, from Proto-West Germanic *hōk, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz. Compare the sense “small cluster of houses” in cognate Dutch hoek.
Low German, to a lesser degree also Central German, variant. From Middle Low German hōrt, hōrde and northern Middle High German horde, both ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *hurdi, *hurþi.

16th century, from Middle Low German *hummer, itself from Old Norse humarr, perhaps through early Norwegian (as many lobsters were caught off the coast of Norway). From the same North Germanic source Modern Low German Hummer, Plautdietsch Humma, Dutch hommer.

16th century, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Middle Low German hump (“heap, lump”), Dutch homp (“chunk, gobbet”), English hump, all possibly from a Proto-West Germanic *hump. Within High German it was originally restricted to the colonial dialects (i.e. East Central German), which might suggest a

From Middle Low German helfte, derived from half (“half”). The form entered Early Modern German via Central German. Equivalent to halb (“half”) + -te. The alternation -b- ↔ -ft- has not been levelled, probably because the same alternation occurs also—for different reasons—in native High German words

From earlier hockern, denominative of Middle High German hucker (“peddler, merchant”), which pertains to Hucke (“load, burden”). The contemporary form is Low German after Middle Low German hȫker. Compare English huckster (borrowed from Dutch) and hawk.

parole.significato: submissive; devout; dependent (especially emotionally and/or sexually, but also in other contexts)
parole.testo: From Middle High German hœrec (“obedient”), equivalent to hören (“to hear, listen, obey”) + -ig. The historic sense after Middle Low German hōrich (“serfish”), derived from the same verb, but probably not (or not primarily) in the sense of “to obey”, but rather “to belong” (for which High German geh

parole.significato: the fabric of a pillow or duvet, which is filled with the downs, etc., and sewn up
parole.testo: 16th century, from Middle Low German inlēde, probably from inlēden (“to insert, fix in, send in”), equivalent to German einleiten. In modern Low German also Inlaat, from Middle Low German inlāten, equivalent to German einlassen, with more or less the same meaning.

Supposedly from Middle Low German gebēte, which is cognate with High German Gebiss (“bit for a horse”), hence “to fasten the reins as on a disobedient horse”. A derivation from Gebet (“prayer”)—possibly in the context of confession—cannot be ruled out, but is considered less likely.
From Middle High German īnsæʒe (“inhabitant, tenant”), from Middle Low German insāte, insēte (“inhabitant”); related to Eingesessener. Ultimately from the root of sitzen (“to sit”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German juche, from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *jūxà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jáušāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *yowHs-ó-s, from *yéwHs. Compare Lower Sorbian jucha, Polish jucha, and Serbo-Croatian juha. Doublet of Jus.

17th century, borrowed from Middle Low German *juchten, juften (16th c.), from Russian юфть (juftʹ), also юхть (juxtʹ), which see for more. The ch-form follows the Russian variant with х, but was likely reinforced by the native Low German variation between -ft- and -cht-. Similarly, the final -en ca

From Middle High German kabel, which is borrowed via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch cabel (“thick rope”), itself from northern French câble. The contemporary sense is from English cable, which see for more.

Circa 1600, from Middle Low German kabbelouw (14th c.), from Middle Dutch cabbeliau, cabelliau (12th c.), from Old Dutch cabillau, possibly from Latin baculum (“stick, staff”), referring to the way cod were split and dried on wooden sticks. Or, with metathesis from/influenced by Basque bakailao (“co

parole.significato: a small flat-bottomed boat such as a punt, used on inland waters
parole.testo: An originally only Central and Low German word, spread by Luther. From northern Middle High German kane and Middle Low German kāne, from Old High German and Old Saxon *kano, all from Proto-West Germanic *kanō, from Proto-Germanic *kanô (“vessel, boat”).

parole.significato: cabin, sleeping quarters (on a ship, barge, yacht, etc. for passengers and officers)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kajüte, which is probably borrowed from Middle Dutch kayhute, though the latter is attested somewhat later. Further origin unsettled; traditionally held to be of Old French origin, according to Watkins, possibly a mix of cabane + hutte. Compare modern Dutch kajuit.
From Middle Low German kamp, from Old Saxon kamp, from Proto-West Germanic *kamp, from Latin campus. Thus originally the same word as Kampf (“fight”).

parole.significato: cinnamon in the form of sticks; (collective) cinnamon sticks
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German kanēl and Middle Low German kaneel, from Middle Dutch caneel, from Old French canele. Cognate with Dutch kaneel, French cannelle.

From Middle Low German kanīneken, diminutive of kanīn, konīn, itself probably through Middle Dutch connijn from Old French connin, northern variant of connil, from Latin cunīculus. Analysable as Kanin + -chen. Compare English cony.

Via Middle Low German kant, kante from Middle Dutch kant, itself from Latin canthus (“tire, edge of a wheel”), from Gaulish *cantos, from Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim”). The Latin spelling is influenced by Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye, tire, etc.”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German kap, from Middle French cap. Compare Dutch kaap, English cape.

parole.significato: to cut down so as to make unusable; to cut off; to interrupt
parole.testo: 17th century, from Middle Low German kappen, from Middle Dutch cappen (“to chop”), perhaps a borrowing from Romansh and from Medieval Latin cappare (“to cut off”), from Vulgar Latin *cappo, from Latin capo (“castrated male chicken”). Compare Alemannic German (Alsatian) kchapfen (“to chop, mince”).

A chiefly Central and Low German form (vis-à-vis Upper German Karren). From Middle Low German karre f and northern Middle High German karre f, from Old Saxon karra and Old High German karra, from Latin carrus (“cart”), from Gaulish *karros. Compare Dutch kar, English car, Swedish kärra. Doublet of R

parole.significato: to chasten (purify spiritually through austerity, asceticism, and/or bodily pain)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German and northern Middle High German kastīen, kastīgen, variant of kestigen, from Old High German kestigōn (“to castigate”), from Proto-West Germanic *kastīgōn. The northern form was spread by Luther.
Borrowed from Middle Low German kerl, from Old Saxon *keril, from Proto-West Germanic *karil. Cognate with Old High German karal. Akin to Dutch kerel, English churl, Old Norse karl, Danish karl.
Borrowed from Middle Low German kesser. A relation with English catch, catcher is possible, though direct borrowing (as assumed by Kluge, edition 24) seems doubtful.

Borrowed from Middle Low German kîken, from Old Saxon kīkan, from Proto-West Germanic *kīkan. The verb is strong in Low German, but treated as weak in standard German. Cognate with Dutch kijken. parole.significato: keel (beam at the underside of a ship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kēl, kil, probably borrowed from Old Norse kjǫlr. Compare Dutch kiel, English keel.

From Middle High German kil, which is possibly a borrowing from the north, from Middle Low German quiele, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to pierce, stick”). Compare somewhat later Lower Rhine Middle Dutch kijl. See quill for more.

16th century, from Middle Low German kime, kimme. This is most plausibly an alteration of kiwe (“jawbone, gill”) after unrelated kimme (“slit, groove”), whence also German Kimme. parole.significato: a large wicker basket, carrying basket (typically on the back)
parole.testo: 15th century, from Middle Low German kīpe. Cognate with dialectal Dutch kiep, English kipe (“basket used for catching fish”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German kimme (“edge; horizon”). Doublet of Kimme. Cognate with Dutch kim (“horizon”).

parole.significato: a notch, particularly in the sight of a firearm
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kimme (“edge; horizon”). Doublet of Kimm. Cognate with Dutch kim (“horizon”).

parole.significato: stub, butt (remnant of a smoked cigarette)
parole.testo: Probably via unattested Middle Low German and Old Saxon forms from Latin cippus (“pole”). The word is attested in early modern German in an Upper German form kipfe and originally meant “top, point”.

From Middle High German kirchhof (“land around a church”). Analyzable as Kirche (“church”) + Hof (“yard”). The semantic development is determined by Middle Low German kerkhof, which came to mean “graveyard” because graveyards have traditionally tended to be established around churches. Compare the s

From a criminal slang word (Rotwelsch) for “house”, which is derived from Middle Low German kōte, whence also German Kate (“hut”). The form Kittchen, though formally a diminutive, is likely to be explained by conflation with unrelated Middle High German kīche (“jail”). Unrelated to English kitchen.

parole.significato: to clap (make a soft clapping sound, particularly of something being closed)
parole.testo: A Central and Low German verb, from Middle Low German klappen, from Old Saxon **klappōn, probably from Proto-West Germanic *klappōn, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną. parole.significato: to clatter (make a rattling or clapping sound)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German klapperen, an iterative form of klappen. Compare Dutch klapperen.
From Middle High German klār, clār, formally from Middle Low German klār or Middle Dutch claer and reinforced by Old French cler, both from Latin clārus (“bright”). Doublet of klaro.
16th c., borrowed from Middle Low German klei, from Old Saxon *klēi, from Proto-West Germanic *klaij.

parole.significato: plumber, tinsmith (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: An originally Central and Low German word, derived from Middle Low German klampe (“clamp”).

parole.significato: rock that is partly covered by (sea) water
parole.testo: From Middle High German klippe, borrowed from Middle Low German klippe or Middle Dutch clippe, ultimately from the root of Kliff (“cliff”). Cognate with Dutch klip, English cliff.

parole.significato: an unofficial school operated privately to teach (poor) children elementary skills
parole.testo: 17th century, from Middle Low German klipschôle (16th c.), probably from klippe (“clog, wooden shoe”) + schôle (“school”). From Middle High German kluoc, which was borrowed via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German klōk and Middle Dutch cloec, from Proto-Germanic *klōkaz. Derived from earlier kneipen, from Middle Low German knīpen, from Old Saxon *knīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *knīpan. Cognate with Dutch knijpen. parole.significato: to crease; to fold; to bend (something that is stable, but not hard, e.g. paper)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German knicken, from Proto-Germanic *knikkōną (“to fold, snap”), which is partly imitative. Cognate with Dutch knikken.

From Knift m or f, a word found in several Central German dialects, sometimes meaning "large knife", sometimes "slice of bread". parole.testo: From the now dated noun Knips (“flip; dab”), itself derived with the northern suffix -s from the verb Middle Low German knippen (“to flip; to slap; to wink”). Compare Dutch knippen. parole.significato: to sizzle; to crackle; to creak; chiefly referring to the sound of fire, or of paper, aluminium, etc., being crumpled
parole.testo: From Middle Low German knisteren, gnisteren. Also a Central German and Dutch word; compare Middle Dutch gnisteren (but modern Dutch knisteren probably from German). Eventually onomatopoeic.

From Middle High German knote, knode, from Old High German knoto, knodo. The two forms are probably variants based on Grammatischer Wechsel. Borrowed from Middle Low German knüppel. Akin to Knopf (“button”).

parole.significato: cabin; berth (sleeping room on a ship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kōje, from Middle Dutch coye, koye, from Latin cavea. Compare Dutch kooi.

parole.significato: scour, pothole (underwater hollow caused by erosion)
parole.testo: 16th century, from Middle Low German kolk, kulk, from Proto-West Germanic *kolk (“hole”), from Proto-Germanic *kulukaz, an extension of *kelǭ (“throat”). Cognate with Dutch kolk. Introduced in standard High German by Luther.

parole.significato: coulter (knife on a plough, fixed in front of the ploughshare)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kolter, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?], from Latin culter. Cognate with Dutch kouter, English coulter.

parole.significato: galley (kitchen of a vessel or aircraft)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kabūse, later influenced by early modern Dutch combuys (now spelt kombuis). The further origin of this word is unsettled.

parole.significato: trading post, factory (branch office of merchants)
parole.testo: Since 16th century, borrowed from Middle Low German kontôr, kuntôr, kumptôr (“commercial branch; writing room; counting desk”), from Middle Dutch contoor, comptoir (modern kantoor), from Middle French contoir, comptoer, from compter (“to count”) + -oir. See English counter for more.
Via Middle Low German or Dutch kurk from early modern Middle Dutch corc, itself from Spanish corcho.

parole.significato: to crawl (typically, but not always, of a baby or insect)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German krabbelen (“to crawl”), an iterative form of krabben (“to scrape”). Compare Dutch krabbelen and krabben. Possibly derived from Krabbe (“crab”). A strong counterargument to this, however, is the cognate krappeln in Middle High German, which did not have the noun.

Via Middle Low German krakēlen from early modern Dutch krakelen (“to quarrel loudly”). Further origin unknown. Most probably derived from Middle Dutch kreel, which is borrowed from Middle French querelle. Other (secondary?) influences may include Dutch kraken (“to crack”) and keel (“throat”).

Kran + Beere. Originally Middle Low German, whence also English cranberry. The English word, on its part, loaned the German word in the rarer sense “cranberry”. Compare Polish żurawina, Latvian dzērvene.

From Middle High German kriusel, derived from krūs, whence modern kraus (“frizzy, curly”). Doublet of Kräusel (“frizzle, squiggle”). From gritteln (“to irritate, bicker, rebuke, nitpick”, 17th c.), which is plausibly an iterative form of Middle Low German gretten (“to anger, irritate”). From Middle Low German krôch, krûch, whence German Low German Kroog and through borrowing Dutch kroeg (“pub”), Swedish krog. Further origin unknown. A relation with etymology 1 cannot be ruled out, but is considered unlikely by most authorities.

parole.significato: the soft part of a baked good which is inside the crust; the crumb
parole.testo: From Middle High German (Central German) krume, reinforced by Middle Low German krume, krōme. See Krümel for more.

parole.significato: crumb (small broken-off piece, particularly of bread)
parole.testo: Old diminutive of Krume, which is now less common in the simplex form. An originally Central and Low German word that has widely replaced the Upper German Brosame in standard usage. From Middle High German (Central German) krume, reinforced by cognate Middle Low German krume, krōme. From Proto-Germa

From Middle High German krüppel, krüpel, borrowed from Middle Low German kröpel, from Old Saxon krupil (“crippled, paralyzed”), from Proto-West Germanic *kruppil. Cognate with Dutch kreupel, English cripple. See there for more.

From a dialectal variant, from Middle Low German kāk (“stake, rod”), Proto-Germanic *kōpǭ (“the prow of a sleigh”), ultimately related to the root of Kegel. Compare Old Norse kafl, kafli (“an elongated, round piece of wood”), Old Norse kefli (“a roll; scroll”), Middle Low German kavele (“cut wood us

A Central and Low German word from Middle Low German [Term?] and northern Middle High German kūle, ultimately from the root of Keule (“club”). The regular High German development is seen in older Kaule, the modern form was introduced via German Low German. Cognate to Dutch kuil, Luxembourgish Kaul.

From Middle High German kunde, künde, from Old High German *kundī (attested in compounds). Abstract noun of the verb künden (“to tell, announce, declare”). parole.significato: an experienced fighter (or activist); a warhorse
parole.testo: Modern (18th century) borrowing from Middle Low German kempe, from Old Saxon kempio; see Kampf. The revived word existed also in an Upper German form: Middle High German kempfe, from Old High German kempho, which is preserved as a surname in the form German Kempf.

parole.significato: to choose individual animals for breeding
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German kören, derived from kēsen (“to choose”). Compare High German küren and kiesen, respectively.

parole.significato: a small piece of hard (chiefly animal) feces
parole.testo: From Middle Low German kötel. Also a Low and Central Franconian word. Cognate with Dutch keutel. Unrelated to German Kot (“feces”); instead, probably derived from the noun at hand in Dutch koot (“little bone”), thus originally “something hard”. Compare German Köte (“the heelbone of a horse; fetlock”

parole.significato: tenant; cotter (farmer who dwells and works on a parcel of a wealthier farmer’s land)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Derived from the noun kotte, kōte (“hut, cottage”), whence German Kate (“hut”). Compare English cotter.

Compound of Küche (“kitchen”) + -n- + Latein (“Latin”). First attested in Middle Low German köken latyn, Köken latin, thus seemingly a popular word ridiculing the improper use of Latin words by the uneducated (such as women and servants in the kitchen). Later used by humanists to refer to non-classi
An originally Central and Low German verb, from Middle Low German labbern (“to drink like a dog; to slurp”). Related to laff (“slack”, here of the tongue).
Borrowed from Middle Low German lāke, from Old Saxon laca, from Proto-West Germanic *laku, from Proto-Germanic *lakō (“lake, pool”). Originally the same word as Lache (“puddle”), which see for more.

parole.significato: sheet; bed sheet (linen used to cover mattresses or furniture, or sometimes instead of a blanket)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lāken, from Old Saxon lakan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“sheet, cloth”). The High German cognate Middle High German lachen, from Old High German lahhan, had already been declining in use when the form Laken was introduced during the pre-eminence of the Dutch and Nor

parole.significato: to land (to reach solid ground in an air, water or space vessel)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German landen, derived from the cognate form of German Land (“land”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Replaced native länden.

parole.significato: to tack (manoeuvre a ship through strong winds)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lavēren, from Middle Dutch laveren, loveren, which is derived from the cognate of German Luv (“windward side of the ship”). It is often supposed that the Dutch verb is borrowed from Middle French lofuyer, from lof (“windward side”), itself a Dutch borrowing in Middle

parole.significato: leak (hole in a large container, such as in a tank)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lek, a nominalization of the adjective leck (“leaky”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German leck, derived from the verb lecken (“to leak”). Compare Dutch lek.

parole.significato: to leak (a liquid, such as water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lecken, from Old Saxon *lekkian, from Proto-West Germanic *lakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *lakjaną, originally a causative of the verb Proto-Germanic *lekaną (“to leak”), related to English leak. The same in Dutch lekken (“to leak”).

parole.significato: leeward side of a ship (the side away from the wind direction)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lē, from Old Saxon hlēo. Cognate with Dutch lij, English lee.

parole.significato: to sail slowly in front the wind
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lensen. Cognate with Dutch lenzen. Perhaps from the same adjective as under etymology 3, though this is not certain.

From Middle High German lest, a contraction of leȥȥest, from Old High German leȥȥist (also laȥȥōst), itself superlative of laȥ (cognate to English late). Borrowed from Middle Low German lichten, originally “to make light”, derived from licht (“light; not heavy”). After the Low German development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte), the verb was merged with, or at least influenced by, unrelated lüchten (“to lift”), from Proto-Germanic *luftijaną, whence als
Borrowed from Middle Low German linnen.

An originally Low and Central German form (though not in all dialects of the latter). From Middle Low German lippe and northern Middle High German lippe, from Old High German *lippa, from Proto-West Germanic *lippjō. One reason for the form’s prevailing in modern standard German was its use in Luthe

parole.significato: a shoot from the stem or roots of a plant
parole.testo: Middle Low German lōde

An originally Central and Low German verb, pertaining to Middle Low German lōde (“sapling”), and hence originally meaning “to grow upward”. The contemporary sense through association with unrelated Lohe (“flame”).

parole.significato: pilot; lodesman (person who helps navigate a difficult waterway)
parole.testo: Shortened from earlier Lootsmann, which is borrowed via Middle Low German lōtsman from Middle English lodesman (“pilot”), cognate with English lode (“waterway”). Compare Dutch loods from the same source.

parole.significato: boggy lowland, moorland, which may seasonally dry and used as a pasture
parole.testo: From Middle Low German lūch, from a West Slavic descendant of Proto-Slavic *lǫgъ (“depression”). Compare Upper Sorbian łuh and Czech luh.
From Middle Low German lucht, just a specification of the general sense of “air” in Luft—as became the primary meaning in English loft.

parole.significato: the windward side of a ship (the side facing the wind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lōf. The contemporary vocalism may be due to the influence of the cognate Dutch loef. See English luff for more.

parole.significato: to mount up from small individual amounts to a large sum
parole.testo: 16th century, from now obsolete lappen (“to slurp”) + -ern (iterative suffix), the former from Middle Low German lāpen (“to slurp”), from Proto-West Germanic *lapōn. The modern sense developed via “to eat [soup] in small sips”. Cognate with Middle High German laffen, Middle Dutch lapen (cf. modern l
From Middle Low German luns(e), from Proto-West Germanic *lunis, see English linchpin. Compare Dutch luns.

Borrowed from Middle Low German mākeler, mēkeler, and Middle Dutch makelare (compare modern Dutch makelaar). There are conflicting statements about whether the Dutch word was borrowed from Low German, or vice versa. The further origin is uncertain, but the word seems to be eventually derived from th

From Middle High German makrēle, from Middle Low German makkerēle, from Middle Dutch makereel, from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown. Compare modern Dutch makreel, modern French maquereau, English mackerel.
From Middle Low German man, a contracting alteration of Old Saxon newan (“none other than”). Compare the similar case of Dutch maar (“only”).
From northern Middle High German manc, inmanc and Middle Low German manc (“among”). Related with German mengen, English among.
Borrowed from Middle Low German marsch, mersch, from Old Saxon mersk, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk.

16th century, alteration of Maseln, borrowed from Middle Low German māselen. Cognate with Middle Dutch masel (“speckle”), whence modern Dutch mazelen (“measles”), and Old High German masala (“lump of blood”). The form with -r- through conflation with Maser (“vein or knob in wood”, etymology 2 below)
Borrowed from Middle Low German merk, from Old Saxon *merk, *merik, from Proto-West Germanic *marik.
Borrowed from Middle Low German merk, doublet of Mark.
From Middle Low German met, from Old Saxon meti (“meal, dish”), from Proto-Germanic *matją, whence also Dutch met. Related with Proto-Germanic *matiz, whence English meat.

parole.significato: bad weather, typically rainy and cold
parole.testo: Technically a compound of Mist (“dung”) + Wetter (“weather”). Mist! is a rather common interjection equivalent to English crap. However, the word is not freely prefixed to nouns, which makes it seem likely that Mistwetter is originally "misty weather", pertaining to Middle Low German mist (“mist”).

From late Middle High German moder (“mold, swamp”), borrowed from Middle Low German modder, modde, mōde (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“dreg”), from Proto-Indo-European *múHtrom. Doublet of Modder (“mud”), a later borrowing. Cognate with Dutch modder.
From Middle Low German mōr, mūr, from Old Saxon mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz, from Proto-Indo-European. Compare Dutch moer, English moor.
Borrowed from Middle Low German mōras, an alteration of Middle Dutch maras on the basis of the predecessor of German Moor (“bog; moor”).

From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German mostert, both from Middle Dutch mostaert, from Old French mostarde. Doublet of Mostrich. Cognate with Luxembourgish Moschter, Dutch mosterd, English mustard, French moutarde.

Borrowed from Middle Low German motte, mutte, from Old Saxon *motta, from Proto-West Germanic *moþþā, perhaps related to *muggju (“mosquito, midge”), or *maþō (“worm”). Cognate with Dutch mot and English moth.

Borrowed from Middle Low German muffen (“to have a moldy smell”), of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to modder (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”). However, compare Old High German *muff (“mold”).

parole.significato: smelly, stinking, particularly: having a moldy smell
parole.testo: The senses "smelly" and "grumpy" go back to different origins. The former pertains to Muff (“bad smell”) from Middle Low German muffen; the latter to Muffel (“grumpy person”), which is an Upper German dialect word of unknown origin. In contemporary German both senses often overlap (see below). It is

parole.significato: theft of food for immediate consumption, which in some jurisdictions is treated as a privileged form of theft (in Germa…
parole.testo: 18th century, from Mund (“mouth”) + Raub (“robbery”), at first in northern authors after Middle Low German mundrôf (early 16th c.).
Borrowed from Middle Low German munkelen (“to speak in private”). Further origin unknown, possibly onomatopoeic, similar to mummeln.
Derived from Middle Low German morken (“to crush; to mash”). Hence also abmurksen (“to murder”). Probably related with morsch (“brittle”).
Loan translation and/or phonetic adaptation of Middle Low German môdersprâke, itself possibly a loan translation of Latin lingua materna. Analyzable as Mutter (“mother”) + Sprache (“language”).

From Middle High German magedichīn, meidichīn, from Old High German *magadihhīn or calqued from Middle Low German mēgedeken, megedekīn, both from Proto-West Germanic *magaþukīn. Equivalent to Magd + -chen.

parole.significato: rubbish, refuse, waste, junk, trash (US), garbage (US)
parole.testo: An originally Central and Low German word from Middle Low German mül (“dust”) and Middle High German mülle, from Old High German mulli (“waste, rubbish”), a nominal formation from mullen (“to crush, grind”), from Proto-Germanic *muljaną (“to crush”) (DWDS).
From Middle Low German mummelen (“to mumble; to talk with one’s mouth full”). Probably related with English mumble, eventually onomatopoeic.
From Middle Low German nā rāde, nā gerāde (“gradually”).

parole.significato: besides; with; in addition to; accompanied by
parole.testo: Shortened from earlier nebens, nebenst, nebest, from Middle Low German nēvens, nēvenst, derived from nēven, cognate of German neben (“next to”).

parole.significato: clove (aromatic flower buds of Syzygium aromaticum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German nēgelke(n) (“little spike, nail”), from Old Saxon nagal (“nail”). Doublet of Nägelchen and Nägelein (archaic). Low German-looking forms are already found in Middle High German negelkīn alongside negelīn; the contraction is first attested in Central German Nelekin. The

Compound of neu (“new”) + gierig (“greedy”), but originally neusgierig with an adverbial genitive. A Middle Low German formation that replaced older Middle High German niugerne. Compare Dutch nieuwsgierig and Norwegian Bokmål nysgjerrig.

Borrowed from Middle Low German nichte, from Old Saxon *nifta, from Proto-Germanic *niftiz. This form replaced High German (obsolete) Niftel in the 17th century. It is based on the Low German shift -ft-→ -cht- (compare Gerücht); hence cognate with Old High German nift, nifta, Dutch nicht, English ni

An originally Low and Central German word from Middle Low German nǖtlīk (“delicious, delicate”) and Central Franconian Middle High German nītlīche, late Central Middle High German niethlīchen (“eagerly”). It is then from Old Saxon niudlīko (“eagerly”) (compare Old English nēodlīċe), Proto-West Germa
From nieder + -ig; probably either borrowed or calqued from Middle Low German nēderich. Cognate to Dutch nederig (“humble”).
Late Middle High German, from Middle Low German noppe, from Old Saxon *hnoppo, from Proto-Germanic *hnuppô (“knot in a fabric; tuft or flock of wool”). Compare Dutch nop, Swedish noppa.

parole.significato: spirit, breath, life (in the sense of Biblical Hebrew רוֹחַ (rûaḥ))
parole.testo: Central and Low German variant of Atem (“breath”) with the widespread dialectal development -ā- → -ō- and unshifted -d-; compare Middle Low German ādem. The form was spread through Luther’s Bible translation but did not replace the Upper German Atem in the everyday sense.

parole.significato: quarter of various units of measure:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German ort (“leftover, remainder, small part, fragment”), from Middle Low German orte (“refuse to eat”), ultimately corresponding to Proto-West Germanic *uʀ- + *etan. Cognate with English ort (“scrap of food, leftover”), Middle High German urez, German uräß.
Borrowed from Middle Low German packe, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

parole.significato: to pack (luggage, a bundle, etc.); to get packed
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German packen, from Old Saxon *pakko, from Proto-West Germanic *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô (“bundle, pack”). Cognate with German Low German packen, Dutch pakken, Saterland Frisian pakje, West Frisian pakke, English pack.
From Middle Low German panēl, probably through Middle Dutch paneel eventually from Old French panel, from Vulgar Latin *pannellus. Doublet of Panel.

parole.significato: skin, peel (mostly in reference to sausages or vegetables, especially potatoes)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German *pelle, whose existence is assured by the word’s prevalence in eastern dialects of German Low German (and East Central German). It was introduced there by Dutch settlers from Middle Dutch pelle, an old borrowing from Latin pellis (“skin”). Compare modern Dutch pel, pellen.

From Middle Low German pōte. Cognate with Dutch poot. The onset pf- through secondary and inadequate adaptation to the Upper German consonantism. (The expected form of a hypothetical cognate would be *pfoße.)

From Middle Low German proppen, prop, borrowed into East Central German and thence into the standard language (early 18th century). The modern form is a secondary adaptation to the Upper German consonantism, based formally on the verb pfropfen (“to engraft”, eventually from Latin propago), which in
From Middle Low German bikbēre, bickbēre. By surface analysis, German Low German Pick (“pitch”) + Beere (“berry”).

parole.significato: pickle (liquid used to preserve food; brine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German pickel, a sub-form of Pökel (“brine for curing”). The ultimate origin is uncertain: perhaps related to the verb picken, from Old Saxon *pikkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn (“to strike”), with influence or intermediary borrowing from French piquer (“to sting, pric

parole.significato: to cheep (of a bird); to squeak (of a mouse)
parole.testo: 16th century, from Middle Low German pīpen, from Old Saxon pīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *pīpan (“to squeak”). Doublet of pfeifen.
From Middle Low German pîr, from Middle Dutch pier, spread by Dutch settlers during the eastern colonisation.
From Middle High German pint, from Middle Low German pint, from Old Saxon *pint, from Proto-West Germanic *pint(i). Cognate with English pintle and German Low German Pint.

From northern Middle High German pissen and Middle Low German pissen, by surface analysis, Pisse + -en. parole.significato: patch, rag of cloth, flat torn-off piece of anything
parole.testo: From Middle Low German and northern Middle High German placke (alongside Upper German pflacke), from Proto-Germanic *plaggą, *plakkô. Cognate with Dutch plak.

parole.significato: plank (big or thick board of wood)
parole.testo: From Middle High German (Central German) and Middle Low German planke, both via northern dialects of Old French, planke, ultimately from Late Latin planca, a vulgar variant of phalanga.

From Middle Low German plump, itself onomatopoeic for a dull fall (as of a stone into water, or a sack on the ground). Cognate with Dutch and Middle Dutch plomp (13th c.), whence also English plump. Alemannic German has shifted forms in Alsatian pflumpfig, Swiss pflumpfet, but these were probably fo
From plumpen + -sen, the former from Middle Low German plumpen (“to fall heavily”). See plump for more.

parole.significato: to fluff up, puff up (principally of birds, but also cats etc.)
parole.testo: Ca. 1600, from Middle Low German plûsteren, iterative of plûsen (“to pick, pluck”). The sense developed from the way that chickens and other poultry groom their plumage. Cognate with Middle Dutch plûusteren; compare also Modern Dutch pluizen. Further origin uncertain; possibly from Old French peluch
In all likelihood derived from Middle Low German plâster (“plaster, pavement”). Thus a doublet of pflastern (“to pave”, also “to hit, smash”).

parole.significato: to flatten, make flat, chiefly by running over or squashing
parole.testo: 18th century, from Low and Central German dialects, ultimately from Middle Low German pletten (“to flatten, smooth”). Cognate with Dutch pletten. By surface analysis, platt + -en.
From Middle Low German plötze (14th c.), from Polabian and/or Old Polish (cf. modern Polish płoć, płotka). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *plotь.

parole.significato: to loot; to plunder; to pillage; to raid (to steal large amounts (from), especially in a state of war or catastrophe)
parole.testo: From Middle High German plundern, plunderen, from Middle Low German plunderen, plünderen, plünren, from Middle Low German plunder, plonder (“robbery, plunder", originally "thing, stuff”), related to Middle Low German plunde, plünde (“junk, stuff, rags, old clothes”), of obscure ultimate origin. 16th century, from Middle Low German pocke, from Proto-Germanic *puhô. Cognate with Dutch pok, English pock. Displaced the variants Poche, Pfoche, which may go back to related Proto-Germanic *puhô, but are perhaps merely inadequate adaptations of the Low German form. The native High German word for
Onomatopoeic, from Middle High German buldern, from Middle Low German bolderen. Compare Polish pultać.
Borrowed from Middle Low German pors, post, from Proto-Germanic *pursaz.
From Middle Low German pot and Middle High German pot (West Central German, 12th century), from Old Saxon *pott, from Proto-West Germanic *pott, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz. See English pot for more.
From Middle Low German prül. Compare Dutch prul (“worthless object”). Further origin unknown.
16th century, from Middle Low German pumpe, pompe, from Middle Dutch pompe. Further origin uncertain, but probably onomatopoeic. Compare English pump.
* Borrowed from Middle Low German pupen.
16th century, from Middle Low German *pūte, imitative of the bird’s (mating) call. Compare German put (with a short vowel), a word used to call chickens and other farm birds (DWDS).

parole.significato: to brine (to preserve food (especially meat) in a salt solution)
parole.testo: From Pökel m (“brine”) + -en, from Middle Low German pekel f (“brine”). Ultimately perhaps from Latin *picco (“to sting”). Compare English pickle.

16th century, from Middle Low German *qualle. Compare modern Low German Quall, Dutch kwal (17th c.). In spite of the earlier High German attestation, the Low German origin is agreed upon for both natural and dialectological reasons. Probably from quellen (like etymology 2 below). However, an alterna
Borrowed from Middle Low German quick, from Old Saxon quik, from Proto-West Germanic *kwiku, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz; also a Central Franconian form. Doublet of keck, which see for more.

parole.significato: yard (horizontal spar on the mast of a sailing ship)
parole.testo: In the nautical sense (17th c.) from Middle Low German râ, raa, from Proto-Germanic *rahō, *raihô. The spellings in -h, -he may have been influenced by dialectal continuations of cognate Middle High German rahe (“pole, bar”), from Old High German raha; though the insertion of -h- in hiatus or at the
Borrowed from Middle Low German rank, ranc, from Old Saxon *rank, from Proto-West Germanic *rank.

From north-eastern Middle High German rase, probably from Middle Low German wrāse (“sod, turf”), though the two could also be cognate forms.
