parole.significato: to race; to speed (drive faster than permitted)
parole.testo: An originally Central and Low German verb, from Middle High German rāsen and Middle Low German rāsen, from Proto-West Germanic *rāsijan (“to race, rush”). Cognates include: Dutch razen, Old English rǣsan (“to hurry”), Old Norse rása (“to move quickly”).

17th century, from Middle Low German *rateren (modern Low German ratern), variant of rettelen, *ratelen, from a frequentative of Proto-Germanic *hratōną. Doublet of German rasseln. See English rattle for more.

parole.significato: tanned furs ready to be processed into clothing
parole.testo: 17th century, from rauch, an obsolete byform of rau (“rough, coarse”, here “hairy”), + Ware (“ware, merchandise”), possibly after earlier Middle Low German rûwāre.
From Middle Low German rêp, from Old Saxon *rēp, from Proto-West Germanic *raip, from Proto-Germanic *raipą, *raipaz. Compare Reif and English rope.
Borrowed from Middle Low German rif, ref, from Old Norse rif.

parole.significato: ray (marine fish with a flat body, large wing-like fins, and a whip-like tail)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German roche, ruche, possibly a derivative of Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz (“rough”), but often thought to be from a substrate (compare also Latin raia). Cognate with Dutch rog, Old English reohhe, ruhha, and, via Old French, English roach (“a fish”).

From northern Middle High German roten, roden and Middle Low German rōden, from Proto-Germanic *rudōną, which is related to *raupijaną (“to rip out, pluck”), *reufaną (“to tear”). Cognate with Dutch rooien. Also akin to English rid, Danish rydde. The variant rotten (still in ausrotten) shows a more
From Middle Low German rotten, alteration (perhaps intensivation) of older rōten, from Old Saxon rotōn, from Proto-West Germanic *rotēn.

parole.significato: to make a low-pitched thudding or tumbling sound (often with a degree of irregularity)
parole.testo: From Middle High German rumpeln, from Middle Low German rumpelen, ultimately onomatopoeic iteratives.
18th century, from Low and Central German dialects. Deverbal from Middle Low German and northern Middle High German ruppen, roppen, cognate of rupfen (“to pluck”), which see.
Borrowed from Middle Low German rüste. Cognate with Dutch rust. Ablaut variant of German Rast, English rest.
From Middle High German schabirnack, from Middle Low German schavernak (14th c.). Further etymology unknown.
Borrowed from Middle Low German schacht, from Old Saxon skaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schaft.

parole.significato: stale (of food and drink: having lost its taste through age, oxidation, etc.)
parole.testo: From (late and northern) Middle High German schal (“tasteless, turbid”), borrowed from Middle Low German schal, from Proto-Germanic *skal-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to dry out”). Compare Swedish skäll (“thin, weak, bleak”), Old English sċeald (“shallow, flat”), whence modern Eng
Borrowed from Middle Low German schorbuk, probably from Old Norse skyrbjúgr. Doublet of Skorbut.
Middle Low German, perhaps from French charte.

From Middle Low German schēle and northern Middle High German schel, from Old High German skelah, from Proto-West Germanic *skelh, from Proto-Germanic *skelhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kel- (“to lean, bend; joint”). The predominant High German form was Middle High German schelch, -hes, Old High

From Middle Low German schellevisch, from schelle (“peel, outer layer”) + visch (“fish”), due either to the relatively large scales or to the layered meat of the fish. The former component is related to German Schale (“peel”), the latter is cognate to Fisch. Compare Dutch schelvis.

parole.significato: to scrub, scour (wash by rubbing with force)
parole.testo: An originally Central and Low German word, from northern Middle High German schiuren and Middle Low German schǖren (both 14th c.). Further origin uncertain, but probably from Old French escurer (“to clean off”), from Late Latin excurare (literally “to treat thoroughly”), from Latin ex- + curare. If
From northern Middle High German schiht, from Middle Low German schicht, schichte, derived from the verb schichten (whence German schichten). Cognate with Dutch schicht, English shift.
From northern Middle High German schihten, from Middle Low German schichten, from Old Saxon *skiftian, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną. Cognate with Dutch schiften, English shift.

parole.significato: skew, oblique, askew, leaning, slanting, aslant, inclined (neither parallel nor perpendicular)
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German schief, schīf (etc.), from Middle Low German schêf, from Old Saxon *skêf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaib, from Proto-Germanic *skaibaz. Regular High German cognates exist only in north-western Central German; compare Central Franconian scheif, northernmost Luxembour
Middle Low German schildepadde, compare Dutch schildpad (“tortoise”).

Derived from etymology 1 due to the similar colour. At first an attributive construction, seemingly of northern origin, in Middle Low German dat scymelinghe perd (1373) and Middle High German ein schemeliges perd (1374, West Central German). Dutch schimmel (“grey horse”) is borrowed from German.

A Central and Low German word, from northern Middle High German *schüppe (attested 15th c.) and Middle Low German schüppe, from Proto-Germanic *skupjō. Cognate with Luxembourgish Schëpp (“shovel”), Dutch schop (“shovel, spade”).

From Middle Low German slagge (“slag”, older “splinter of hammered iron”, 14th c.), from slān (“to hit, strike”), the cognate of German schlagen. Compare Dutch slak, English slag, both also from Middle Low German.

From Middle Low German slap (“flaccid”), from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), and from the same family of words as German *slēpaną (“to sleep”); see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”). parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, whence probably also Dutch sluw. Further origin uncertain. parole.significato: silt (very fine kind of mud found at the ground and shore of some waters)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slik, slīk. Akin to Dutch slik, slijk.

parole.significato: to fishtail, to sway, to roll (to move in uncontrolled manner shaking from side to side) (of a ship, car or other vehic…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German slingeren, iterative of slingen, which latter is cognate with German schlingen, English sling. The iterative also in Dutch slingeren.

parole.significato: to sleep lightly or briefly; to doze; to slumber
parole.testo: An originally Low and Central German word, from northern Middle High German slummen and Middle Low German slummeren, slommen, from Old High German *slūmēn, from Proto-Germanic *slūm-. Cognate with Dutch sluimeren, English slumber.

parole.significato: need, privation, especially hunger or thirst
parole.testo: From rare, northern Middle High German smaht, later reinforced by Middle Low German smacht. Derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“little, small”). Related to Schmach.

parole.significato: to suffer hardship, especially severe hunger or thirst
parole.testo: First attested in the 17th century, from Schmacht + -en, after Middle Low German smachten. parole.significato: power, force, vigour, especially when hitting or moving something heavy
parole.testo: From the Low and Central German verb schmacken (“to hit hard”), ultimately of imitative origin; compare Middle Low German smacken. This verb is cognate with English smack, which see for more.

Borrowed from Middle Low German snak (“speech, chatter”), from Middle Low German snacken (“to speak, talk, chatter”), akin to Middle High German snacken (“to chatter, chat”).

parole.significato: skra (kind of medieval legal document in northern Germany and around the Baltic Sea)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schrā, itself probably from Old Norse skrá (“parchment”), though it might also be inherited from the underlying Proto-Germanic *skrahō.

parole.significato: to hatch (shade an area with fine lines)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German schrafferen, from Middle Dutch schraeffeeren, from Italian sgraffiare (“scratch”).

parole.significato: to grate or peel (vegetables) with a blade (knife, peeler)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schrap(p)en (14th c.), borrowed from Middle Low German schrāpen, from Proto-West Germanic *skrapōn.

Deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną.

parole.significato: to shove, to push, to hustle
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. See schubsen for more.

parole.significato: swath, windrow (row of cut grain or hay; both cut out herbage and the left empty space)
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German swade and Middle Low German swade, both from Proto-Germanic *swaþō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swey- (“to bend, turn, swing”). See English swath for more.

parole.testo: Sometimes taken as a loan from Middle Low German, but first attestations are nearly contemporaneous (1514 for Low German, 1543 for High German, according to Grimm). From Middle Low German swimelen, iterative of Middle Low German swīmen (“to swoon”). Cognate with Dutch zwijmelen, obsolete German schweimeln.

From Middle High German sigel and Middle Low German seg(g)el, both from Latin sigillum. Compare Dutch zegel.

parole.significato: a swampy gorge, a brook in a valley
parole.testo: From Middle Low German sîpe, from the verb sîpen (“to trickle”). Cognate with Middle High German sīfe, whence the alternative forms, and further with Dutch zijp (“canal, sewer”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German so vōrt, from so (intensifier) + vōrt (“forth; soon”). Written as one word from the 16th century.
From Middle High German sol, sul, borrowed from Middle Low German sōle, sāle (“saltwater, brine”). Cognate with German Low German Söle, Sööl (“brine, pickling”).

parole.significato: a sort, variety, grade of a good produced for sale or consumption
parole.testo: In general use since the 16th century. Borrowed from Middle Low German sorte (14th c.), from Old French sorte, and from chiefly independent Upper German sorta, sort (15th c.), from Italian sorta; all eventually from Latin sors. See English sort for more.

parole.significato: thin, scrawny (having an unusually low amount of both muscle and fat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German spak (“thin, dry, brittle”) from spake (“brushwood”). Or from rare Middle Low German spak (“tame, calm”) from an unknown source.
Borrowed from Middle Low German span, from Old Swedish spander, Swedish spann.

From Middle Low German spille, from a contraction of Proto-West Germanic *spinnilu (“spindle”). Doublet of Spindel.

Borrowed from Middle Low German splinte.

parole.significato: collective word for apparitions or actions of ghosts, haunting, supernatural (usually frightening) occurrences
parole.testo: 17th century, from Middle Low German spōk, from Old Saxon *spōk, from Proto-Germanic *spōk. Cognate with Dutch spook, whence English spook.

parole.significato: country, state (politically constituted legal person wielding absolute power of a population and territory)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German stāt, from Middle Dutch staet, probably via Old French estat from Latin status. The semantic development was influenced by cognate modern French état. Doublet of Status and Etat.

From Middle Low German stāpel, from Old Saxon stapol, from Proto-West Germanic *stapul (“pillar, post, basis, foundation”). Doublet of Etappe and Staffel.
Partial calque of Middle Low German statelīk, from state. Compare Dutch statelijk, Swedish ståtlig and Norwegian statelig.

parole.significato: a post to which an offender is tied in order to be flogged publicly
parole.testo: 13th century, from northern Middle High German stūpe, from Middle Low German stûp, staup, from Polabian staup, from Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”).
From northern Middle High German stellemacher, reinforced by Middle Low German stellemāker. Equivalent to a prefixless byform of Gestell (“rack, frame”) + Macher (“maker”).

parole.significato: score, a set of twenty, e.g. of sheaves, livestock, eggs

Since the 15th century, probably from Middle Low German stūr(e) with influence from German Stier. Doublet of stur.

parole.significato: stripe, weal, wale, a linear pattern on skin, as resulting from a violent lash

parole.significato: to tie (someone) to a post and flog them publicly
parole.testo: 16th century, from Staupe (“post for public flagellation”), from Middle Low German staup, stûp, from Polabian staup, from Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ (“post, pillar”).

parole.significato: bungler, botcher, slacker (someone who habitually performs badly, due to lack of skill or care)
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German stümper. Derived from the cognate of Stumpf (“stump”). Cognate with Dutch stumper.

parole.significato: a square or spot in a village that historically served as a thingstead

parole.significato: to tap, to strike lightly (often repeatedly)

From Middle High German tiuschen, from a Middle Low German dialect, cognate with tauschen (“to trade”), with both terms of unknown further origin.

parole.testo: From a merger of dialectal tolp (with variants; of unknown, probably onomatopoetic, origin) and Middle High German dörpel, itself dissimilated from dörper, from Middle Low German dorper (“villager”), from dorp (“village”). parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German uchte, from Old Saxon ūhta, from Proto-Germanic *unhtwǭ. Related to Dutch ochtend (“morning”).
